t.5.1: Arjuna said: O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions, and then again yoga. Tell me with certainty that one of these two which is the better.
t.5.2: The Blessed Lord said: Renunciation and the yoga of action both lead to the highest good; but of the two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.
t.5.3: He who neither hates nor desires should be known as one who is ever a renouncer; for, O mighty-armed one, free from the pairs of opposites, he is easily released from bondage.
t.5.4: It is the childish, not the wise, who speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as different. One who is properly established in even one of them obtains the fruit of both.
t.5.5: The state that is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is reached by the followers of Yoga as well. He who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one, he truly sees.
t.5.6: But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is hard to attain without yoga; the sage who is yoked in yoga attains Brahman before long.
t.5.7: One who is joined in yoga, pure in self, self-controlled and master of his senses, whose self has become the self of all beings, is not tainted even while acting.
t.5.8: "I do nothing at all," so should the one who is disciplined and knows the truth think, even while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, walking, sleeping, and breathing.
t.5.9: Even while speaking, letting go, grasping, opening and closing the eyes, he holds firmly that it is only the senses that are moving among the objects of the senses.
t.5.10: One who acts, placing all actions in Brahman and abandoning attachment, is not stained by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not stained by water.
t.5.11: With the body, with the mind, with the intellect, and even with the senses alone, yogins perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the purification of the self.
t.5.12: The disciplined man, having abandoned the fruit of action, attains lasting peace; the undisciplined man, attached to the fruit through the force of desire, is bound.
t.5.13: Having renounced all actions with the mind, the self-controlled embodied one dwells happily in the city of nine gates, neither acting at all nor causing action.
t.5.15: The all-pervading Lord does not take on anyone's sin, nor indeed anyone's good deed. Knowledge is veiled by ignorance; by that, living beings are deluded.
t.5.14: The Lord does not create agency for the world, nor actions, nor the union of action with its fruit; it is one's own nature that sets all this in motion.
t.5.16: But for those in whom that ignorance has been destroyed by knowledge of the Self, that knowledge, like the sun, illuminates the Supreme.
t.5.17: Those whose understanding is fixed on That, whose very self is That, whose steadfast devotion is to That, and who hold That as their supreme goal go to the state from which there is no return, their impurities shaken off by knowledge.
t.5.18: The wise see with an equal eye a brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, and even a dog and an outcaste who cooks dogs.
t.5.19: Even here in this world, creation is conquered by those whose mind is established in equality; for Brahman is flawless and equal, and therefore they are established in Brahman.
t.5.21: He whose self is unattached to external contacts finds the happiness that lies within the self; his self joined in the yoga of Brahman, he attains imperishable happiness.
t.5.20: One should not rejoice on obtaining what is pleasant, nor be troubled on meeting what is unpleasant; steady in understanding and free from delusion, the knower of Brahman abides in Brahman.
t.5.22: For the pleasures that are born of contact with the senses are indeed sources of sorrow; they have a beginning and an end, O Kaunteya, and the wise man does not delight in them.
t.5.23: He who is able, here in this very world, before release from the body, to withstand the surge born of desire and anger, he is a disciplined man, he is a happy man.
t.5.25: The seers whose sins are destroyed, whose doubts are cut asunder, who are self-controlled and who delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
t.5.26: For the ascetics who are freed from desire and anger, whose minds are controlled and who have known the Self, the extinction in Brahman exists all around them.
t.5.27: Shutting out external sense-contacts and fixing the gaze between the eyebrows, making equal the inward and outward breaths that move within the nostrils,
t.5.28: The sage whose senses, mind and intellect are controlled, who is wholly devoted to liberation, and from whom desire, fear and anger have departed, he is truly liberated forever.
t.5.29: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.
t.5.24: He who is happy within, who rejoices within, and who likewise is illumined within, that yogī, having become one with Brahman, attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
